🐛 Bug
Problem
PyTorch reports its version as a string, which is hard to compare. In addition to that, with the upcoming release of 1.10, version comparison is going to have a silent bug.
Below are some problems with the current version reporting
Comparing 1.1x -- incorrect result after comparison
Because this behavior is silent, it might be a potential bug.
>>> "1.10" < "1.3.0"
True

Comparing to version tuples -- Error as we report a string
This issue fails, so might be OK. However, it would still be nice to be able to compare the versions and tuples
>>> torch.__version__ < (1, 3, 0)
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'tuple'
>>> torch.__version__
1.9.0+cu102

Resolution 1. Use  python's version parser directly, and return the built-in Version class
>>> from packaging import version
>>> version.parse("1.10") < version.parse("1.3.0")
False
>>> version.parse("1.9.0+cu102") < version.parse("1.3.0")
False
>>> version.parse("1.9.0+cu102") > version.parse("1.3.0")
True
>>> type(version.parse("1.9.0+cu102"))
packaging.version.Version

The main problem with this resolution is that it expects the users to compare the instances of the packaging.version.Version.
Resolution 2. Report version as a tuple
>>> (1, 9, 0, 'cu102') < (1, 3, 0)
False
>>> (1, 10) < (1, 3, 0)
False

I think this is a better way, as it follows the style that is returned by the python's sys.version_info. However, this does not follow the pattern used by NumPy.

🚀 Feature
Proposal to allow Dict[str, Tensor] as an input/output type when exporting torchscript models to ONNX.
Motivation
Both ONNX and onnxruntime support non-tensor inputs/outputs i.e. Sequences and Maps, it would be very useful if PyTorch could export models which utilized this.
ONNX models are completely stateless in inference mode, this means that any state which could have been updated in a torchscript model using setattr/getattr, instead needs to be passed through the model explicitly as an an additional input/output. In complex scenarios where state consists of many tensors of various shapes/sizes, managing this could be made much simpler if the state could be contained as a Map/Dict object.
Alternatives

Having many variables representing inputs/outputs of a model, although this quickly becomes unmanageable
Another alternative is to trace the model which allows dictionary of inputs, by implicitly mapping them to separate inputs of the ONNX graph at export time, but then we still have to deal with many discrete inputs to the session at runtime, and lose the flow control with scripting provides us.

Additional context
Is this feature currently on the ONNX roadmap, and if not, what are the potential blockers for someone that might want to look into implementing this?

This issue describes a problem with Python dependencies and a potential solution. The goal is to start a discussion to decide whether (and if so, how) to resolve this problem; that may end up being via the proposal below or via a different approach.
Problem
Currently, we use many different Python dependencies (primarily installed via pip or conda) for many different jobs in CI. These dependencies are spread all across the repository (the following list probably isn't comprehensive):

.circleci/

docker/common/install_conda.sh
verbatim-sources/job-specs/

job-specs-custom.yml
pytorch-job-specs.yml




.github/

templates/

linux_ci_workflow.yml.j2
windows_ci_workflow.yml.j2


workflows/

lint.yml
test_tools.yml




.jenkins/pytorch/

win-test-helpers/

build_pytorch.bat
setup_pytorch_env.bat


macos-test.sh


Makefile
requirements-flake8.txt
requirements.txt

This makes it very difficult to correctly add new Python dependencies that are used in CI, such as #60658.
Furthermore, some of these dependencies are pinned to specific versions, but others are not. This sometimes causes CI to break when dependencies are upgraded: for instance, see #60472 which pinned numpy to version 1.20 to fix our mypy lint. Notice that that PR only pins mypy in one place and nowhere else, compounding the fragmentation (as an aside, notice in that multiple numpy versions are already pinned in the section of install_conda.sh linked above).
In addition to complicating CI, this also makes local development more difficult. For example, after #60658 was merged, several PyTorch developers ran into errors when running tests locally because they did not have expecttest installed on their development machines. There is no automated system in place to help PyTorch developers ensure that they have all the Python packages they need to do their work.
Proposal
The draft PR #60697 prototypes the following approach:

Add a requirements-dev.in file which includes (via -r) our existing top-level requirements*.txt files, and also specifies several other dependencies which we currently use in CI but only buried inside of scripts.
Use pip-compile to automatically generate a .circleci/docker/requirements.txt file from that requirements-dev.in file, which pins everything
Use a GitHub Actions job to run pip-compile to make sure .circleci/docker/requirements.txt stays up to date. This doesn't update pinned dependencies; it only ensures that the generated file reflects the requirements-dev.in file it's generated from.
Wherever possible, replace hardcoded pip install (or even conda install) commands with pip install -r .circleci/docker/requirements.txt.
Use a separate GitHub Actions job to submit PRs to bump pinned dependencies in .circleci/docker/requirements.txt via pip-compile --upgrade.

This has a few downsides/caveats:

From initial experiments, it seems to take up to a minute to run pip install -r .circleci/docker/requirements.txt in GitHub Actions. This isn't great compared to our previous approach to install specific packages (which would only take a few seconds), but it's also not terrible.
Reviewing the autogenerated pip-compile --upgrade PRs could be tedious.

cc @ezyang @seemethere @malfet @walterddr @pytorch/pytorch-dev-infra

When using large models with DDP, we witness two NCCL all reduces per iteration and have no ability to increase the first bucket size.  This is due to reducer.hpp KDefaultFirstBucketBytes being a const expr int that cannot be modified through the python api, yet it is exposed as an attribute of torch.distributed.
The value is defined here:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/reducer.hpp
    
    
         Line 26
      in
      43fb39c
    
  
  
    

        
          
           constexpr int kDefaultFirstBucketBytes = int(1024 * 1024); 
        
    
  


The bucket size is set here:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/reducer.cpp#L1649
There is a Python API exposure, however since the value is a constexpr it is defined at compile time which would make changing it through Python at Runtime problematic. Changing the value through the Python does not currently work.
Python API:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/init.cpp
    
    
         Line 1623
      in
      43fb39c
    
  
  
    

        
          
           module.attr("_DEFAULT_FIRST_BUCKET_BYTES") = ::c10d::kDefaultFirstBucketBytes; 
        
    
  


The user should be able to increase this KDefaultFirstBucketBytes value through the python API.
Reproduction Steps (Should Work in any pytorch container from 21.05 and onwards):

tar -xvzf ddp_overlap.tgz
cp -r ddp_overlap /opt/
cd /opt/ddp_overlap
bash run.sh

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
DepthFirstGraphNodeIterator is a class which facilitates easy iteration over the IR, which is a very nice utility.
It also currently makes uses of a good amount of state which is unnecessary. There is block_stack_, graph_, and current Block contained in BlockIteratorPair current_. However, every node has a unique next node in a Depth First iteration which is determinable just form the node itself.
To quote from comment on original PR:

I think the only member variable the iterator needs to keep around is the current node. From the node you can recover the current block with node->owningBlock(), and you can recover the block's owner with block->owningNode() (which will be null if it's the graph block). Based on the current block/node you can recover what the next node to be searched in depth first order is, e.g. if the current node's is the last node in first block of an if node, then we'll need to search the second block of the if node next.

Motivation
We should encourage more use of DepthFirstGraphNodeIterator, and concurrently also clean it up a bit so we're not doing things less efficiently than we could.

A model during conversion to ONNX is duplicated by converter. It seams that the new tensors are created as copies of the tensors in the PyTorch model. It temporary doubles the model RAM usage. It means that you needs 2xRAM to convert model than to just do inference with it. It vastly limits practical applications of very large ONNX models or requires workaround with manual split of model structure before it is converted to ONNX.
To Reproduce
Modify this script to use 60% of your RAM for inference and run it:
import torch
import math

# Size in GB
tensor_size = 4
print("Tensor size ", tensor_size, "GB")
# Change this to ~60% of your RAM size
model_size = 16
print("Model size ", model_size, "GB")
# The number of layer will be adjusted to fit in less than model size
layers_num = model_size // tensor_size
kB = 1024
MB = kB * kB
GB = MB * kB
#Number size
precision_size = 4
activation_size = math.floor(math.sqrt(tensor_size * GB / precision_size))
print("Activation size ", math.floor(activation_size / kB * precision_size), "kB")

class Net(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, empty_init = False):
        super(Net, self).__init__()
        for i in range(layers_num):
            name = "fc_%d" % i
            linear = torch.nn.Linear(activation_size, activation_size)
            setattr(self, name, linear)
    def forward(self, x):
        for i in range(layers_num):
            name = "fc_%d" % i
            linear = getattr(self, name)
            x = linear(x)
        return x

model = Net()


print("Model created")

input = torch.zeros(activation_size, requires_grad=True)
output = model(input)

🚀 Feature
Please refer to the forum link below for my initial question.
https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/sequential-inference-of-multiple-models-in-a-memory-limited-environment/125517
I would like to request a feature to allow multiple models to be used on the same data while only using the minimum amount of memory necessary for running each model without having to load all the models to CPU and GPU memory. This feature is important for deployment and I believe that TorchScript should have this feature.
Motivation
In deployment situations, we sometimes find it necessary to apply multiple models on the same data. The first model might be a style transfer network for converting the scene to a reference style, the second may be a detection network for vehicles within the style-transferred image, and the third network may be a classification network for an ROI extracted by the detection network. While the example given above is fictitious, the problem of applying multiple models to the same data occurs frequently in deployment.
However, if the size of each model is large and there are many models, it becomes impossible to load all the necessary models in memory. Assuming that each model has 1GB of parameters and that there are 20 separate models, it becomes necessary to load 20GB to RAM, which may be larger than the allocated hardware can manage.
Currently, Tensorflow graph mode manages the necessary memory automatically so that only the minimum necessary host and device memory are allocated during inference. This means that even if 20 models are being used, only the necessary models are actually loaded from disk to memory in RAM and GPU. Also, the next necessary model is loaded from disk to GPU while the previous model is still performing calculations on GPU, which removes latency,
It is possible to do this in Python as well by manually scheduling the process. However, loading the next model and transferring to GPU while the current model is executing in Python may be inefficient since the GPU calculations may be finished before the next model is sent to GPU. Using multi-threading is impossible due to the GIL and using multi-processing is error-prone.
Another alternative would be to merge the models to perform multi-task prediction and use techniques such as knowledge distillation to reduce model size. However, having separate models often has higher performance and provides modularity in execution. Also, even if smaller models are created, having to make space for all models is problematic.
Pitch
Currently, TorchScript is focused on deploying a single model on a stream of data. However, I believe that many deployment scenarios involve applying multiple models on any single input, which is why I request this feature. I am aware that this would take much effort to implement. Also, I do not think that this feature is necessary for dynamic execution.
Alternatives
Using the C++ API?
cc @gmagogsfm

🚀 Feature
Make the warning message about the default OMP_NUM_THREADS set by torch.distributed.launch and torch.distributed.run use logger.warning(msg) rather than a print statement.
Motivation
Users can set the LOGLEVEL environment variable when using torch.distributed.launch and torch.distributed.run CLI utils to control the python log level of the launcher program. However regardless of the overriden LOGLEVEL the following message prints:
$ python -m torch.distributed.run ~/test.py

*****************************************
Setting OMP_NUM_THREADS environment variable for each process to be 1 in default, to avoid your system being overloaded, please further tune the variable for optimal performance in your application as needed.
*****************************************

This is because in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/distributed/run.py#L523-L530 the message
is printed using print(msg) rather than log.warning(msg).
Pitch
Simply change the print() to log.warning().
Alternatives
N/A - simple change.
Additional context
Came up as part of the discussion #60716 (comment). The OMP message was left untouched for backwards compatibility and in torch<1.9.0 torch.distributed.launch used to not support user-overrides for LOGLEVEL (in torch-1.9.0 it does). Now that users do have an option to pass a custom LOGLEVEL it makes sense to make the OMP printout a log.warning so that users only interested in LOGLEVEL=ERROR don't have to see this message every time.
nodes.title: torch.distributed.launch/run - make OMP warning message a log.warning rather than a stdout print

🚀 Feature

We'd like the Constant Propagation pass to have a special handling for the dequant node to
transform the pattern:
Constant fp32_weight -> quant -> dequant
to:
Constant int8_weight -> dequant.
Motivation

In the int8 JIT workflow, we will insert quant and dequant after the weight tensor to construct the int8 fusion pattern. In addition, we want to mark the weight as Constant during inference so that we could do more optimizations like weight cache.
After inserting the quant, dequant node and freezing the module, we will have the below pattern:
Constant fp32_weight
        |
      quant
        |
     dequant
        |
       conv

The current Constant Propagation path will transform this pattern into:
Constant fp32_weight
        |
       conv

which breaks our fusion pattern needed.
Pitch

We'd like to have the below transformation before and after Constant Propagation:
Before:
Constant fp32_weight
        |
      quant
        |
     dequant
        |
       conv

After:
Constant int8_weight
        |
     dequant
        |
       conv

Alternatives


We tried to set preserveParameters=True when doing the freezing, but the weight will no longer be marked as Constant on the graph.
We have checked the JIT quantization flow of PyTorch, we found that PyTorch will firstly freeze the module, insert quant/dequant, do the fusion on the graph to fuse quant->op->dequant into q_op, and then the ConstantPropagation etc. It is possible that we follow this flow as well, except that we also want to get the concrete shape information. However, it seems that we could only get these info at runtime, as a result, the ConstantPropagation will happen before our CustomPasses at runtime, and the CP will remove the dequant and quant on the Constant weight.
